title: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives

fields.label: Label
fields.value: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Extinction caused by Natural Selection”. Scope: varieties and species, wild and domesticated

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted kinship gradient can be tested in modern replacements and fossil turnovers. Existing data mainly provide observational proxies and poorly capture the full process during new-species formation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For invasions, radiations and replacement events, test whether decline or extinction risk rises with phylogenetic and niche similarity to the expanding form. Disproportionate losses among nearest relatives support the prediction; losses unrelated or negatively related to kinship refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Close relatives may facilitate one another or differ ecologically despite kinship.

Direct observations of speciation coincident with competitor extinction are rare.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.57
analysis feasibility: 0.64
discriminating power: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.76
data existence: 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Relatedness and co-occurrence can be combined for plants and for better-known fossil clades, which is a real but partial design. The prediction is close to Darwin's naturalization hypothesis and can be scored with existing floras and trees. Competition is inferred from overlap and decline, and those patterns have other causes, so the test is informative mainly as a comparative proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: When a form expands or a non-native species establishes, compare the decline of closest relatives with the decline of distant co-occurring taxa, in fossils and in modern assemblages. Greater impact on sister lineages would confirm the claim; impact that is independent of relatedness, or stronger on distant natives, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fossil sister-species pairs are rarely resolved.

Invasions often hit naive distant taxa harder than close relatives, which cuts against a simple test.

Co-occurrence and replacement are not direct measures of competition.

data existence: 0.64
